quote: But experiment has shown that the more detailed subjects’ visualization, the more optimistic (and less accurate) they become.
content: The essay does not tell anyone to stop planning. It says, in so many words, "When you want to get something done, you have to plan out where, when, how," and it reserves the outside view for the forecast. Koole and van't Spijker's result is that distinction, measured: implementation intentions sped completion and made the predictions even more optimistic (Koole & van't Spijker 2000). Plan with the inside view and predict with the outside view. That is the division of labor the essay draws, and it is the one the data support.

quote: Just ask how long similar projects have taken in the past, without considering any of the special properties of this project.
content: Kahneman and Lovallo, who introduced the inside/outside distinction, told forecasters to anchor on the outside view because people adjust away from it in the direction of optimism (Kahneman & Lovallo 1993). Reference-class forecasting as governments adopted it applies uplifts read from the distribution of past overruns for that type of project (Flyvbjerg 2006). It does not invite the promoter to argue that this project is special. The combination the note prefers works when the adjustment is disciplined, and the essay's "without considering any of the special properties" is advice for readers who have no such discipline and whose adjustments go one way. Base rates are priors, and the essay's epistemology says priors should be updated on evidence. A planner's feeling that this time is different is not evidence.

quote: Are they symptoms of bureaucracy or government incentive failures? Yes, very probably.
content: The essay concedes exactly this, and Fable concedes that it concedes. What the objection adds is that the essay "spends the essay on the lab result." The lab result is what tests the cognitive account on its own. Students estimating their own theses have no promoter rewarding low bids, and more than half of them still missed their own 99 percent deadline (Buehler, Griffin & Ross 1994). Flyvbjerg's later work puts project overruns down to both strategic misrepresentation and optimism bias, weighted by how political the setting is (Flyvbjerg 2008, European Planning Studies). The essay picked the half that applies to its readers, who are more likely to plan a term paper than an airport.
